header: IN THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH AT KARACHI
Petitioner : Through Mr. Muhammad Naseer, Advocate.
J U D G M E N T
body: Abdul Hamid Bhurgri, J.- The petitioner has invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, challenging the consolidated judgment dated 02.07.2024, passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.XII (Model Civil Appellate Court), Karachi South, in First Rent Appeal Nos.108 and 93, whereby the petitioner’s appeal seeking enhancement of fair rent was dismissed, while the respondent’s appeal was partly allowed by modifying the judgment dated 13.03.2024, passed by the learned Rent Controller in Rent Case No.169 of 2023, and reducing the fair rent of the demised premises from Rs.25,000/- to Rs.16,000/- per month.

2. Briefly, the petitioner, being one of the co-owners of property bearing Survey No.21, Sheet No.SB-7, situated in Marvi Building, Mochi Gali/Stalker Street, Saddar, Karachi, filed an application under Section 8 of the Sindh Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (hereinafter referred to as “the Ordinance”), seeking fixation of fair rent in respect of Shop No.B-11, Ground Floor, measuring approximately 180 square feet. The respondent was occupying the premises as a tenant at a monthly rent of Rs.7,920/-, excluding other charges. The petitioner asserted that the existing rent was substantially below the prevailing rent of comparable commercial premises in the same building and adjoining locality, which, according to him, ranged between Rs.50,000/- and Rs.60,000/- per month. He also relied upon inflation, increased construction and maintenance costs, property taxes and annual rental value. It was further alleged that the respondent had ceased making direct payment of rent after September 2018. Accordingly, fixation of fair rent at Rs.60,000/- per month was sought.

Page 2 of 7 3. The respondent contested the application, denying the claimed prevailing market rent and the alleged increase in taxes, repair and maintenance expenses. Both parties led evidence and were subjected to cross-examination. The petitioner produced, inter alia, a tenancy agreement (Exh.A/3) relating to Shop No.C-16, situated in the same building and stated to measure approximately 180 square feet, reflecting monthly rent of Rs.34,000/-. The respondent questioned its genuineness, principally on the ground that the agreement mentioned 01.11.2022, whereas the stamp paper was issued on 15.11.2022, and that neither its executant nor any marginal witness had been examined. Upon consideration of the evidence, the learned Rent Controller, vide judgment dated 13.03.2024, allowed the application and fixed the fair rent at Rs.25,000/- per month with effect from January 2023, being the month of institution of the rent application, with further enhancement subject to Section 9 of the Ordinance.

4. Both parties preferred appeals against the aforesaid determination. The petitioner sought further enhancement, whereas the respondent challenged the increase. The learned Appellate Court, through the impugned consolidated judgment dated 02.07.2024, dismissed the petitioner’s appeal and reduced the fair rent to Rs.16,000/- per month, maintaining its applicability from the date of institution of the rent application. Aggrieved thereby, the petitioner has approached this Court, seeking fixation of fair rent at Rs.50,000/- per month or, alternatively, between Rs.34,000/- and Rs.40,000/- per month.

5. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the learned Appellate Court failed to properly appreciate the commercial location of the demised premises, the prevailing rental value of comparable shops and the evidence available on record. Particular reliance was placed upon Exh.A/3, relating to Shop No.C-16, situated in the same line and having approximately the same area as the demised premises. He explained that 01.11.2022 represented the commencement of tenancy, whereas the agreement was formally executed on 15.11.2022, before the Justice of Peace. Thus, according to learned counsel, the apparent discrepancy regarding the dates did not justify rejection of the document.

Page 3 of 7 Learned counsel further referred to the admissions made by the respondent’s attorney during cross-examination that the demised premises was situated in a commercial area, near Zaibunnisa Street, Saddar Cooperative Market and Bohra Bazar, and that Shop No.C-16 was situated in the same line. The attorney also admitted that the rent had not been increased for approximately six years. Although he claimed that the respondent was occupying the premises under a Pagri arrangement, no supporting agreement or documentary evidence was produced. Learned counsel argued that the reduction of fair rent to Rs.16,000/- was arbitrary and contrary to the material on record. In support of his submissions, he relied upon PLD 2022 Sindh 52, 2023 SCMR 1147 and 2024 SCMR 781.

6. Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent supported the impugned appellate judgment and contended that the petitioner had failed to establish the statutory considerations prescribed under Section 8 of the Ordinance. He submitted that Exh.A/3 was not proved through its executant or marginal witnesses and that the discrepancy in its dates rendered it unreliable. He further argued that no documentary evidence was produced regarding increased property taxes, construction or repair costs, or enhancement in the annual rental value. According to learned counsel, the petitioner was essentially seeking reappraisal of evidence, which was impermissible in constitutional jurisdiction, particularly after availing the statutory remedy of appeal under Section 21 of the Ordinance. He, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the petition with costs, relying upon 2009 YLR 1124, 2008 CLC 517, 2008 CLC 610, 2019 YLR 2765, 2013 YLR 2541, PLD 2005 Karachi 554 and 1998 CLC 963.

7. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and examined the material available on record. The controversy requiring determination is whether the learned Appellate Court was justified in reducing the fair rent from Rs.25,000/- to Rs.16,000/- per month and whether such interference warrants correction in constitutional jurisdiction.

8. Section 8 of the Ordinance empowers the Rent Controller to determine fair rent after taking into consideration the rent of Page 4 of 7 similar premises situated in similar circumstances in the same or adjoining locality, the rise in construction and repair costs, the imposition of new taxes, if any, and the annual value of the premises on which property tax is levied. The Honourable Supreme Court has emphasized that determination of fair rent requires consideration of the statutory parameters with reference to the particular characteristics of the premises, including their location, nature, size and comparable rental circumstances, and that no uniform formula can be applied indiscriminately . This Court has further held that it is not mandatory for all four considerations enumerated under Section 8 to be established cumulatively; satisfactory proof of even one relevant statutory consideration may justify determination or enhancement of fair rent . The exercise must, nevertheless, rest upon a fair and reasonable assessment of the evidence rather than conjecture or an arbitrary estimate.

9. In the present case, the commercial character and location of the demised premises are not seriously disputed. The respondent’s attorney admitted during cross-examination that the shop is situated in a commercial locality of Saddar, Karachi, near established commercial markets, and that Shop No.C-16, relied upon by the petitioner for comparison, is situated in the same line. Both shops are stated to measure approximately 180 square feet. These circumstances are material because Section 8(1)(a) expressly recognizes the rent of comparable premises situated in similar circumstances in the same or adjoining locality as a relevant consideration for determining fair rent.

10. The principal objection concerning Exh.A/3 relates to the difference between the date mentioned in the agreement, namely 01.11.2022, and the date of issuance of the stamp paper and its stated execution, namely 15.11.2022. Learned counsel for the petitioner explained that the former date represented the commencement of tenancy, whereas the latter was the date on which the agreement was formally executed. Such an explanation cannot be regarded as inherently improbable, since commencement of tenancy Messrs Haque Traders and others v. Sheikh Abid & Co. (Pvt.) Ltd. and others (PLD 2024 Supreme Court 918).
Moinuddin Paracha v. Messrs Novartis Pharma Pakistan Ltd. and others (2015 YLR 947, Sindh High Court).

Page 5 of 7 and execution of its written instrument need not necessarily coincide. The discrepancy, therefore, required examination in the context of the document as a whole and could not, by itself, be treated as conclusive proof of its invalidity or fabrication.

Admittedly, the executant and marginal witnesses of Exh.A/3 were not examined, and its evidentiary value must consequently be assessed with appropriate caution. Nevertheless, the document was required to be considered along with the other material circumstances, particularly the admitted commercial location, proximity and comparable area of the two shops. While Exh.A/3 may not conclusively establish the precise prevailing market rent, the learned Appellate Court was required to evaluate its evidentiary worth in conjunction with the surrounding circumstances rather than allowing the discrepancy in dates alone to assume decisive significance.

11. It is equally important to observe that the petitioner did not produce sufficient documentary evidence to establish the alleged increase in property taxes, construction and repair expenses or annual rental value. No affirmative finding can, therefore, be recorded in his favour on those grounds. However, the absence of such evidence does not necessarily defeat an application under Section 8 where another relevant statutory consideration is satisfactorily established. The admitted commercial location of the premises and the evidence relating to a comparable shop in the same building were relevant circumstances requiring due consideration. The respondent’s assertion regarding a Pagri arrangement was likewise unsupported by documentary evidence and could not, by itself, furnish a basis for reducing the fair rent.

12. The learned Rent Controller, after recording the evidence of both parties, determined the fair rent at Rs.25,000/- per month. Significantly, despite the petitioner’s claim of Rs.60,000/- and the higher comparable rent reflected in Exh.A/3, the learned Rent Controller did not mechanically adopt either figure. Instead, a substantially lower amount was fixed, reflecting a measured assessment of the material placed before him. The learned Appellate Court was undoubtedly competent to examine the correctness of that determination; however, its interference required adequate reasons Page 6 of 7 demonstrating why the assessment was erroneous or inconsistent with the statutory considerations. The reduction from Rs.25,000/- to Rs.16,000/- per month, in the circumstances of the present case, has not been supported by a sufficiently reasoned evaluation of the relevant material, particularly the comparable commercial location, area of the premises and the evidence relating to Shop No.C-16.

13. It is settled law that constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199 is neither appellate nor revisional in character. This Court cannot undertake a fresh appraisal of evidence or substitute its own opinion merely because another conclusion may also be possible. Interference is, however, permissible where the findings of a subordinate forum suffer from misreading or non-reading of material evidence, misapplication of law, perversity or jurisdictional error resulting in miscarriage of justice . In the present case, interference is warranted not for undertaking an independent assessment of market rent, but because the learned Appellate Court failed to adequately address material considerations relevant to the exercise under Section 8 of the Ordinance and thereby disturbed a determination which was reasonably supported by the available record.

14. Having considered the matter within the aforesaid limited jurisdiction, I am of the view that the fair rent of Rs.25,000/- per month fixed by the learned Rent Controller represents a reasonable and balanced assessment of the material available on record. The said determination neither accepts the petitioner’s substantially higher claim nor disregards the commercial character and comparable rental circumstances of the premises. Conversely, no sufficient legal or factual justification has been demonstrated for reducing the fair rent to Rs.16,000/- per month. There is, therefore, no occasion either to enhance the rent to the amount claimed by the petitioner or to sustain the reduction made by the learned Appellate Court.

15. For the foregoing reasons, this constitutional petition is partly allowed. The consolidated judgment dated 02.07.2024, passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.XII (Model Civil Moinuddin Paracha v. Messrs Novartis Pharma Pakistan Ltd. and others (2015 YLR 947, Sindh High Court), particularly the discussion concerning the limited scope of interference under Article 199 in rent matters.

Page 7 of 7 Appellate Court), Karachi South, in First Rent Appeal Nos.108 and 93, is set aside to the extent that it reduced the fair rent of the demised premises from Rs.25,000/- to Rs.16,000/- per month. Consequently, the judgment dated 13.03.2024, passed by the learned Rent Controller in Rent Case No.169 of 2023, fixing the fair rent at Rs.25,000/- per month with effect from January 2023, is restored, subject to the provisions of Section 9 of the Ordinance. Any amount already paid or deposited towards rent for the relevant period shall be duly adjusted. The parties shall bear their own costs. JUDGE Ayaz Gul
